title: Separate wind-change slopes gave no clear forecast gain in offshore Atlantic and eastern Pacific windows in 2003-2023
abstract: We tested whether separate slopes after storm strengthening and weakening improve next-day wind-change estimates. We used NOAA IBTrACS v04r01 and fitted each test season from earlier seasons. In 1,655 offshore Atlantic windows from 133 storms, the added absolute-history term increased mean squared error by 0.10%. The conditional 95% three-year season block interval for error reduction was -0.41% to +0.17%. In 2,871 eastern Pacific windows from 222 storms, error rose by 0.43%, with an interval of -1.05% to +0.38%. One planned secondary comparison gave a gain: when the eastern Pacific base already had squared history, adding absolute history reduced error by 0.77%, with limits of 0.24% to 1.46%. The primary test gives no clear gain for a simple split in response slope. It does not show equal physical persistence. Future sample selection, revised best tracks, simple models and fixed-prediction uncertainty limit use. The package includes code, aggregate scores, fitted coefficients, source hashes and a figure. Source records stay outside the baseline publication.

display.caption: MSE reduction from separate strengthening and weakening slopes in five planned tests per basin. Positive values mean lower error. Bars show conditional 95% three-year season block intervals. The eastern Pacific comparison against squared history is positive; primary comparisons are uncertain.

citations.reason: Published sample and history-model benchmark informed this new response-slope test. Atlantic source data overlap; this is not independent confirmation.
